Embedding models turn text into vectors whose distances track meaning, and most of the cost of serving them is not the arithmetic but the movement of data around it. A request arrives as text, is split into tokens on the host, copied to the device, looked up in an embedding table, passed through a stack of attention layers, pooled into one vector per row, normalized, and copied back. Each of those steps can be a separate kernel launch or a separate allocation, and each copy between host and device costs time that the model itself never needed. A library that keeps the pipeline on the device, fuses the small steps into their neighbours, and reports every byte that crosses the bus lets a caller see where the time goes instead of guessing. The same library can then run on a laptop with no accelerator at all, using plain kernels on the CPU, and give the same token ids and vectors within a published tolerance, so that code written on a developer's machine behaves the same way in production. When a device cannot honor an option, the call fails and names the option, rather than quietly doing something else. When a caller is willing to trade a little accuracy for speed, the library says how much accuracy was traded, measured against the reference, not estimated. None of this needs a framework or a graph interpreter at run time; it needs a small, exact contract between the caller, the model bundle, and the hardware. A second machine, on a different device and a different build, runs the same tokenizer over the same bytes and must reach the same token ids before it computes a single vector, because a tokenizer that drifts by even one position changes every vector after it, and no amount of numerical tolerance in the arithmetic that follows can repair a row that was never the row the model was evaluated on in the first place.
